Bank of America released a new investor report today pointing out that Meta's newly launched Muse AI agent app highlights how third-party AI agents are gradually bypassing Apple's ecosystem and posing a threat to its services revenue. Below are the details.

Bank of America maintains a 'Buy' rating

Apple's stock price fell more than 2.5% today after Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan released an investor report warning that AI agents like Meta's Muse could increasingly take over product search, recommendations, and transactions currently conducted through the Apple ecosystem.

The following is an excerpt from his report, republished via SeekingAlpha:

Mohan's report came as Meta's Muse has sat firmly atop the US App Store's free app chart for nearly two weeks. According to estimates from Sensor Tower cited by TechCrunch, Muse had surpassed 3.4 million downloads as of last week.

Meta's OpenClaw-like AI agent app can browse the web, fill out forms, book travel, send emails, and make online purchases on behalf of users, and it appears to be hugely popular with the general public, having climbed to the top of the US App Store in just 10 days, surpassing ChatGPT.

Returning to Mohan's report, he maintained his 'Buy' rating on Apple with a US$370 target price, saying that despite the new risks posed by AI agents, he still看好 Apple becoming the 'ultimate winner in endpoint AI.'

The following is an excerpt from his report, republished via Yahoo! Finance:

Mohan also noted that Muse's list of merchant integrations continues to expand, including Shopify and Shop Pay, Expedia, and PayPal — all examples of how AI agents are increasingly able to handle everything from product search to checkout.

In addition, Mohan mentioned that current iPhones already have sufficient computing power to run AI agents, so for Apple, software execution and integration are the bigger challenges.

Mohan pointed out in his report that Apple's services, chips, payments, privacy, and Siri AI teams must accelerate their coordinated efforts for the company to compete in what he calls the 'user intent economy.'

Top-voted comment posted by FishWhisperer

If you ask people whether they'd be willing to hire a complete stranger and give them access to all your accounts and credit cards so they can handle all your affairs to save you time, most would say no. Even for people they claim to 'trust,' they might not agree. Yet when it comes to letting an agent app do the same thing, they seem to have no such reservations. My view is that when many people's agent apps spin out of control or get hacked, they'll face painful lessons, because there have already been reports saying this kind of situation happens very easily.

Specifically regarding Siri AI, he also pointed out that Siri lacks some of Muse's capabilities, including persistent background-running tasks, broad third-party action support, and dedicated agent payment channels.

He also mentioned the difference in development pace between the two: Apple typically releases a major software update only once a year, while AI agents can 'improve every single day.'

However, Mohan believes Apple's massive installed base of devices and its privacy-focused reputation are its key advantages, especially crucial in convincing users to entrust sensitive tasks to AI agents.

Have you used AI agents like Muse? Feel free to share your experience in the comments section.
